units.description: Calculus-based kinematics: position, velocity, acceleration as derivatives/integrals; projectile and circular motion.
units.note:
# Unit 1: Kinematics

## Overview
**Kinematics** describes motion without yet explaining its causes. In AP Physics C: Mechanics, this unit builds motion from **calculus**: **position**, **velocity**, and **acceleration** are connected through **derivatives** and **integrals**, and these ideas are applied to **one-dimensional motion**, **projectile motion**, and **uniform circular motion**.

This unit matters because AP questions often test whether you can move fluently between **graphs, equations, and physical interpretation**, especially using calculus to connect changing motion quantities.

---

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | The object’s location as a function of time, usually written as $$x(t)$$, $$y(t)$$, or $$\vec{r}(t)$$ | Often the starting point for deriving velocity and acceleration from a function |
| **Velocity** | The rate of change of position; a vector quantity | AP problems frequently ask for velocity from a position function or from the slope of a graph |
| **Acceleration** | The rate of change of velocity; also a vector | Central to interpreting motion and connecting kinematics to later dynamics |
| **Derivatives in motion** | Using calculus to find instantaneous rates: slope of $$x(t)$$ gives $$v(t)$$, slope of $$v(t)$$ gives $$a(t)$$ | Core AP Physics C skill: using derivatives rather than only constant-acceleration formulas |
| **Integrals in motion** | Accumulated change: area under $$v(t)$$ gives displacement, area under $$a(t)$$ gives change in velocity | Frequently tested through graph-based free-response and multiple-choice questions |
| **Constant-acceleration motion** | Motion where $$a$$ is constant, allowing closed-form equations | These equations remain useful, but AP often expects you to know when they do **not** apply |
| **Projectile motion** | Two-dimensional motion with independent horizontal and vertical components | A classic AP topic: students must separate axes and apply kinematics independently |
| **Uniform circular motion** | Motion in a circle at constant speed with changing direction | Important because acceleration exists even when speed is constant; connects to centripetal acceleration |

---

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Position function $$\vec{r}(t)$$"] --> B["Differentiate to get velocity $$\vec{v}(t)=\dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$$"]
    B --> C["Differentiate to get acceleration $$\vec{a}(t)=\dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt}=\dfrac{d^2\vec{r}}{dt^2}$$"]
    C --> D["Interpret direction and magnitude of motion"]
    C --> E["Integrate acceleration to recover velocity change"]
    B --> F["Integrate velocity to recover displacement"]
    D --> G["Apply in 1D motion"]
    D --> H["Resolve into components for projectile motion"]
    D --> I["Identify inward acceleration in circular motion"]
```

A useful AP workflow is:

1. Start with the given representation: **equation**, **graph**, or **verbal description**.
2. Identify the relevant quantity: $$\vec{r}(t)$$, $$\vec{v}(t)$$, or $$\vec{a}(t)$$.
3. Use **derivatives** to move to rates of change or **integrals** to recover accumulated change.
4. In two dimensions, break motion into **independent components**.
5. Check whether acceleration is **constant** before using shortcut kinematics equations.

---

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Relationship** | **Formula** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Average velocity** | $$\bar{v}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$$ | Overall rate of position change over an interval |
| **Instantaneous velocity** | $$v=\frac{dx}{dt}$$ | Slope of the position-time graph |
| **Average acceleration** | $$\bar{a}=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ | Overall rate of velocity change |
| **Instantaneous acceleration** | $$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$$ | Slope of the velocity-time graph |
| **Displacement from velocity** | $$\Delta x=\int_{t_i}^{t_f} v(t)\,dt$$ | Area under a velocity-time graph |
| **Velocity change from acceleration** | $$\Delta v=\int_{t_i}^{t_f} a(t)\,dt$$ | Area under an acceleration-time graph |
| **Constant-acceleration position** | $$x=x_0+v_0 t+\frac{1}{2}at^2$$ | Valid only when $$a$$ is constant |
| **Constant-acceleration velocity** | $$v=v_0+at$$ | Basic constant-acceleration relation |
| **Velocity-position relation** | $$v^2=v_0^2+2a(x-x_0)$$ | Useful when time is absent and $$a$$ is constant |
| **Projectile horizontal motion** | $$x=x_0+v_{0x}t$$ | Horizontal acceleration is typically zero |
| **Projectile vertical motion** | $$y=y_0+v_{0y}t-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$$ | Vertical motion under gravity |
| **Component velocities** | $$v_{0x}=v_0\cos\theta,\qquad v_{0y}=v_0\sin\theta$$ | Resolving launch velocity into axes |
| **Uniform circular speed** | $$v=\frac{2\pi r}{T}=\omega r$$ | Speed around a circular path |
| **Centripetal acceleration** | $$a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2 r$$ | Direction is always toward the center |

**Key definitions to remember:**
- **Displacement** is change in position, not total path length.
- **Speed** is the magnitude of velocity.
- **Velocity** and **acceleration** are **vectors**, so direction matters.
- In ideal projectile motion near Earth’s surface, $$a_x=0$$ and $$a_y=-g$$.

---

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Critical Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Position vs. displacement** | Both describe location-related quantities | **Position** is where an object is; **displacement** is the change between two positions |
| **Velocity vs. speed** | Speed is based on velocity magnitude | **Velocity** includes direction; **speed** does not |
| **Average vs. instantaneous quantities** | Both describe motion rates | **Average** uses a finite interval; **instantaneous** uses a derivative at a single moment |
| **Projectile motion vs. circular motion** | Both are two-dimensional motion problems | **Projectile motion** usually has constant downward acceleration; **circular motion** has inward radial acceleration |

You can also think of the calculus relationships this way:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Graph of $$x(t)$$"] --> B["Slope gives $$v(t)$$"]
    B --> C["Slope gives $$a(t)$$"]
    C --> D["Area gives $$\Delta v$$"]
    B --> E["Area gives $$\Delta x$$"]
```

---

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **displacement** with **distance traveled**. A negative displacement does not mean a negative distance.
- Using constant-acceleration formulas when acceleration is **not constant**. If $$a$$ changes with time or position, use calculus.
- Forgetting that an object in **uniform circular motion** has nonzero acceleration even if its **speed** is constant.
- Mixing horizontal and vertical quantities in **projectile motion** instead of treating axes independently.
- Misreading graph questions: the **slope** of a graph and the **area under** a graph represent different physical quantities.

---

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can define **position**, **displacement**, **velocity**, **speed**, and **acceleration** precisely.
- [ ] I can compute $$v(t)$$ from a given $$x(t)$$ using $$\frac{dx}{dt}$$.
- [ ] I can compute $$a(t)$$ from a given $$v(t)$$ or $$x(t)$$ using derivatives.
- [ ] I can use integrals or graph areas to find **displacement** or **change in velocity**.
- [ ] I can identify when the **constant-acceleration equations** are valid.
- [ ] I can analyze **projectile motion** by separating horizontal and vertical components.
- [ ] I can explain why **uniform circular motion** involves **centripetal acceleration** toward the center.
- [ ] I can move between **equations, graphs, and verbal descriptions** of motion without losing the physical meaning.

--- 

If you want, I can also turn this into a **one-page cram sheet** or a **lesson-by-lesson preview guide** for Unit 1.

flashcards.definition: A time-dependent quantity that specifies an object's location relative to a chosen origin. In one dimension, its slope with respect to time gives velocity.
The rate of change of position with respect to time at a specific moment, given by $$v(t)=\frac{dx}{dt}$$.
The rate of change of velocity with respect to time, equivalently the second derivative of position: $$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$$.
The change in position over an interval, computed as final location minus initial location, or from velocity by $$\Delta x=\int_{t_i}^{t_f} v(t)\,dt$$.
A set of motion relationships valid when acceleration does not vary with time, such as $$v=v_0+at$$ and $$x=x_0+v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A particle moves along the $$x$$-axis with position $$x(t)=3t^3-5t^2+2t+1$$, where $$x$$ is in meters and $$t$$ is in seconds. What is the particle's acceleration at $$t=2\,\text{s}$$?
A particle has velocity $$v(t)=4t^2-6t+1$$ for $$0\le t\le 3$$. What is the displacement from $$t=0$$ to $$t=3\,\text{s}$$?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For motion in one dimension, if acceleration is given as a function of time, velocity can be found from $$t_i$$ to $$t_f$$ using ______.
For one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration, the position as a function of time is ______.

flashcards.definition: Two-dimensional motion under uniform downward acceleration in which horizontal and vertical components are analyzed independently, neglecting air resistance.
The relationship between vertical and horizontal coordinates for launched motion under gravity, obtained by eliminating time from the component equations.
The component of acceleration parallel to the instantaneous direction of motion, responsible for changing the speed of an object along its path.
The inward component of acceleration for curved motion, with magnitude $$\frac{v^2}{r}$$, directed toward the center of curvature.
Motion along a circular path at constant speed, in which the acceleration changes only the direction of the velocity vector and points radially inward.

multipleChoice.questionText: A projectile is launched from ground level with speed $$v_0$$ at angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, neglecting air resistance. Which expression gives the total time the projectile remains in the air before returning to the launch height?

A car moves counterclockwise around a flat circular track of radius $$20\,\text{m}$$. At one instant its speed is $$10\,\text{m/s}$$ and increasing at $$3\,\text{m/s}^2$$. What is the magnitude of its total acceleration at that instant?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For a projectile launched from and landing at the same height with initial speed $$v_0$$ at angle $$\theta$$, the horizontal range is ______.
For motion along a circle of radius $$r$$ with speed $$v$$, the inward radial acceleration has magnitude ______.

units.description: Newton's three laws using calculus, variable forces, friction, and constraint problems with multiple bodies.
units.note:
# Unit 2: Newton's Laws of Motion

## Overview
This unit develops **Newton’s three laws of motion** as the core framework for analyzing how forces change motion, especially in systems with **multiple objects**, **friction**, and **variable forces**. For the AP Physics C: Mechanics exam, this unit is essential because many free-response and multiple-choice questions require building correct **free-body diagrams**, applying $$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$, and using **calculus** when forces depend on position, velocity, or time.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Newton’s First Law** | An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. | Helps identify when $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$ and whether acceleration is zero. Often used in equilibrium or constant-velocity situations. |
| **Newton’s Second Law** | The net force on an object equals the time rate of change of momentum; for constant mass, $$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$. | This is the main equation for force problems, including connected objects, inclined planes, and variable-force motion. |
| **Newton’s Third Law** | Forces between two interacting objects come in equal-magnitude, opposite-direction pairs acting on different objects. | A common AP trap is mixing up third-law pairs with forces that cancel on the same object. |
| **Free-Body Diagrams** | Diagrams showing all external forces acting on a chosen object. | Essential for setting up equations correctly. Most AP mechanics errors begin with a poor free-body diagram. |
| **Friction** | Contact force opposing relative motion or impending motion: static or kinetic. | Students must distinguish $$f_s \le \mu_s N$$ from $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ and know friction direction from motion tendency. |
| **Constraint Problems** | Problems involving strings, pulleys, or connected bodies where motions are linked. | AP questions often require relating accelerations and tensions across a system before applying Newton’s laws. |
| **Variable Forces** | Forces that depend on $$x$$, $$v$$, or $$t$$ rather than being constant. | Physics C expects calculus-based reasoning, such as solving $$m\frac{dv}{dt} = F(x)$$ or relating force to acceleration dynamically. |
| **Mass vs. Weight** | **Mass** measures inertia; **weight** is the gravitational force, usually $$mg$$ near Earth. | Important for distinguishing what changes between locations and for writing force equations correctly. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose the object or system] --> B[Draw a complete free-body diagram]
    B --> C[Choose coordinate axes]
    C --> D[Resolve forces into components]
    D --> E["Apply Newton's Second Law in each direction"]
    E --> F[Add constraint relations if multiple bodies are connected]
    F --> G[Use friction rules if contact forces are present]
    G --> H[Include calculus if force or acceleration varies]
    H --> I[Solve for acceleration, tension, normal force, or motion]
    I --> J[Check sign, direction, and physical reasonableness]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Law / Rule** | **Expression** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Newton’s First Law** | $$\sum \vec{F} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{a} = 0$$ | If the net external force is zero, velocity is constant. |
| **Newton’s Second Law** | $$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$$ | Most general form; especially useful conceptually. |
| **Constant-mass form** | $$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$ | Main working equation in this unit. |
| **Momentum** | $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ | Connects force to changing motion. |
| **Weight** | $$\vec{W} = m\vec{g}$$ | Gravitational force near Earth. |
| **Static friction** | $$f_s \le \mu_s N$$ | Adjusts up to a maximum value to prevent slipping. |
| **Maximum static friction** | $$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$ | Used at the threshold of motion. |
| **Kinetic friction** | $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ | Applies when surfaces slide relative to each other. |
| **Spring force** | $$F_s = -kx$$ | Restoring force; sign shows opposition to displacement. |
| **Acceleration definition** | $$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$$ | Important when combining Newton’s laws with calculus. |
| **Net force with variable force** | $$m\frac{dv}{dt} = F(x,t,v)$$ | General setup for non-constant-force problems. |
| **Component form** | $$\sum F_x = ma_x,\qquad \sum F_y = ma_y$$ | Usually the most effective way to solve AP force problems. |

### Key force-model reminders
- **Normal force** is not always equal to $$mg$$; it depends on the situation.
- **Tension** is the pulling force in a string; in ideal massless strings over frictionless pulleys, tension is often the same throughout one string.
- On an incline, weight is often resolved into:
  $$
  mg\sin\theta \quad \text{parallel to the incline}, \qquad mg\cos\theta \quad \text{perpendicular to the incline}
  $$

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Pair** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Static friction vs. Kinetic friction** | **Static friction** prevents slipping and can vary up to $$\mu_s N$$; **kinetic friction** acts during sliding and is usually modeled as constant $$\mu_k N$$. | Students often incorrectly set $$f_s = \mu_s N$$ in every static case. |
| **Mass vs. Weight** | **Mass** is inertia and stays constant; **weight** is the gravitational force $$mg$$ and depends on the gravitational field. | Critical when interpreting scales, elevators, inclines, and non-Earth contexts. |
| **Action-reaction pair vs. balanced forces** | A **third-law pair** acts on two different objects; **balanced forces** act on the same object and sum to zero. | One of the most tested conceptual distinctions in mechanics. |
| **Single-object analysis vs. system analysis** | A **single-object** approach reveals internal contact forces like tension or normal force; a **system** approach can eliminate internal forces. | AP free-response questions often reward choosing the more efficient model. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Single object] --> B[See all external forces clearly]
    A --> C[Useful for tension or normal force]
    D[Whole system] --> E[Internal forces cancel]
    D --> F[Useful for finding overall acceleration]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **Newton’s Third Law pairs** with forces that cancel. Third-law forces act on **different objects**, so they do not cancel in one free-body diagram.
- Assuming the **normal force** is always $$N = mg$$. On an incline or with vertical acceleration, this is generally false.
- Setting **static friction** equal to $$\mu_s N$$ automatically. In many problems, static friction is **less than** its maximum value.
- Forgetting to define a consistent positive direction before writing equations, leading to sign errors in acceleration and force components.
- Treating connected objects as having unrelated motions when a **constraint** from a string or pulley requires equal-magnitude accelerations or linked displacements.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can state and apply **Newton’s three laws** in words and equations.
- [ ] I can draw a correct **free-body diagram** for an object on a surface, incline, or in a pulley system.
- [ ] I can write and solve $$\sum F_x = ma_x$$ and $$\sum F_y = ma_y$$ using well-chosen axes.
- [ ] I can distinguish **mass**, **weight**, **normal force**, **tension**, and **friction** in a force analysis.
- [ ] I can determine whether to use $$f_s \le \mu_s N$$ or $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ and choose the correct friction direction.
- [ ] I can analyze **multiple-body systems** and apply motion constraints from strings and pulleys.
- [ ] I can handle **inclined-plane problems** by resolving forces into components.
- [ ] I can set up Newton’s Second Law with **calculus** for a **variable force**, such as $$m\frac{dv}{dt} = F(x)$$ or $$F = m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$$.

flashcards.definition: A frame of reference in which an object with zero net external force moves with constant velocity, so the standard form of Newtonian dynamics applies directly.
The vector sum of external interactions on an object equals the time rate of change of its momentum; for constant mass, this is $$\sum \vec{F}=m\vec{a}$$.
A representation that isolates one object and shows all external interactions acting on it as vectors, allowing application of component equations in chosen axes.
The contact interaction parallel to a surface that adjusts in magnitude to prevent relative slipping, up to a maximum value of $$f_s\le \mu_s N$$.
The contact interaction parallel to a surface during sliding motion, with magnitude modeled by $$f_k=\mu_k N$$ and direction opposite relative motion.

multipleChoice.questionText: A block of mass $$m$$ is pushed along a horizontal surface by a force of magnitude $$F$$ applied at an angle $$\theta$$ below the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $$\mu_k$$. What is the block's horizontal acceleration?
A box remains at rest on a rough incline of angle $$\theta$$. Which statement about the friction force is correct?
options: Its magnitude must equal $$mg\sin\theta$$ as long as equilibrium is possible.
Its magnitude is zero because the box does not move.
Its direction is always down the incline.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Its magnitude must equal $$mg\sin\theta$$ as long as equilibrium is possible.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For a particle of constant mass, Newton's second law in vector form can be written as $$\sum \vec{F}=m\,\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$$. The missing quantity is ______.
A block is just about to slip on a horizontal surface. At that instant, the friction force magnitude is ______.

flashcards.definition: The pulling interaction transmitted through an ideal light string, acting along the string's length; in an ideal massless string over frictionless pulleys, its magnitude is uniform throughout a connected segment.
A relationship among positions, velocities, or accelerations imposed by system geometry, reducing the number of independent variables in connected-body problems.
An interaction whose magnitude or direction changes with position, velocity, or time, requiring application of dynamics with functions rather than constants.
For an ideal spring, the restoring interaction is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction, given by $$F_x=-kx$$.
Two interactions of the same type between different objects that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, consistent with Newton's third law.

multipleChoice.questionText: Two blocks, $$m_1$$ on a frictionless table and $$m_2$$ hanging vertically, are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the system?
A particle moves along the $$x$$-axis under a net force $$F(x)=bx$$, where $$b$$ is a positive constant. Which statement is correct?
options: The acceleration is proportional to $$x$$ and in the positive $$x$$-direction when $$x>0$$.
The acceleration is constant because $$b$$ is constant.
The particle must move with constant velocity when $$x=0$$.
The force is a restoring force toward the origin.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The acceleration is proportional to $$x$$ and in the positive $$x$$-direction when $$x>0$$.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For an ideal spring displaced by $$x$$ from equilibrium along the $$x$$-axis, the spring force is ______.
Two masses connected by a taut, inextensible string over an ideal pulley must have accelerations with equal ______.

units.description: Work as a line integral, kinetic and potential energy, conservation of energy, and power for variable forces.
units.note:
# Unit 3: Work, Energy, and Power

## Overview
This unit develops the **work–energy framework** for analyzing motion, especially when forces vary with position. You will connect **work as a line integral**, **kinetic and potential energy**, **conservation of mechanical energy**, and **power** to solve problems efficiently on the AP Physics C: Mechanics exam.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Work** | Energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement; for general motion, work is a **line integral**. | AP questions often test whether you can compute work for **variable forces** or determine when work is positive, negative, or zero. |
| **Net Work–Kinetic Energy Theorem** | The total work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. | This is one of the most powerful shortcuts for relating force and motion without directly using kinematics. |
| **Conservative Forces** | Forces for which work depends only on initial and final positions, not the path. | Essential for identifying when **potential energy** can be defined and when **mechanical energy is conserved**. |
| **Potential Energy** | Energy associated with position in a conservative force field. | AP problems often ask you to move between **force functions** and **potential energy graphs/equations**. |
| **Conservation of Mechanical Energy** | When only conservative forces do work, the sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant. | A central exam tool for springs, gravity, loops, ramps, and variable-height motion. |
| **Nonconservative Work** | Work done by forces like friction or applied forces that changes mechanical energy. | AP free-response questions frequently include friction and require energy accounting with **external or dissipative work**. |
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. | Tested in both average and instantaneous forms, especially with **variable forces** or speed-dependent situations. |
| **Force–Potential Relationship** | Conservative force is related to potential energy by the negative spatial derivative. | Important for interpreting graphs and deriving equilibrium behavior from **$$U(x)$$**. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify system] --> B[Identify forces]
    B --> C{Are all relevant forces conservative?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Use mechanical energy conservation]
    D --> E["$$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$$"]
    C -->|No| F[Include nonconservative work]
    F --> G["$$W_{nc} = \Delta K + \Delta U$$"]
    G --> H[Relate position, speed, and energy changes]
    E --> H
    H --> I{Need rate of energy transfer?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Use power relations]
    I -->|No| K[Finish problem]
    J --> L["$$P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$"]
    L --> K[Finish problem]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Idea** | **Equation / Rule** |
|---|---|
| **Work by a constant force** | $$W = \vec{F}\cdot\Delta \vec{r} = F\Delta r\cos\theta$$ |
| **Work by a variable force** | $$W = \int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$$ |
| **One-dimensional work** | $$W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F_x(x)\,dx$$ |
| **Net Work–Kinetic Energy Theorem** | $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$$ |
| **Kinetic energy** | $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ |
| **Gravitational potential energy near Earth** | $$U_g = mgy$$ |
| **Spring potential energy** | $$U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ |
| **Conservative-force definition** | $$W_c = -\Delta U$$ |
| **Mechanical energy** | $$E_{\text{mech}} = K + U$$ |
| **Mechanical energy conservation** | $$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$$ |
| **With nonconservative work** | $$W_{nc} = \Delta E_{\text{mech}} = \Delta K + \Delta U$$ |
| **Instantaneous power** | $$P = \frac{dW}{dt}$$ |
| **Power from force and velocity** | $$P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$ |
| **Average power** | $$P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$$ |
| **Force from potential energy in one dimension** | $$F_x = -\frac{dU}{dx}$$ |

### Must-know interpretations
- The **area under a graph of $$F_x$$ vs. $$x$$** gives **work**.
- The **slope of a graph of $$U$$ vs. $$x$$** gives **negative force**.
- If a force is **perpendicular** to displacement, then its work is $$0$$.
- A conservative force transfers energy between **$$K$$** and **$$U$$** without changing total mechanical energy.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Work vs. Power** | **Work** is total energy transferred; **power** is the rate of transfer. | Students often calculate the correct work but forget that power also depends on **time** or **instantaneous velocity**. |
| **Conservative vs. Nonconservative Forces** | Conservative forces have path-independent work and allow a potential energy function; nonconservative forces do not. | Critical for deciding whether to use **$$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f$$** directly or include **$$W_{nc}$$**. |
| **Force graph vs. Potential energy graph** | For **$$F_x(x)$$**, area gives work. For **$$U(x)$$**, slope gives force through **$$F_x=-dU/dx$$**. | A frequent AP graph-analysis theme. |
| **Net work vs. Individual force work** | **Net work** changes kinetic energy; individual forces may exchange energy differently. | Helps avoid mistakes when normal force, gravity, friction, and applied forces all act together. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Force function $$F_x(x)$$"] --> B["Integrate over position"]
    B --> C["Work: $$W=\int F_x\,dx$$"]
    D["Potential energy $$U(x)$$"] --> E["Differentiate with respect to position"]
    E --> F["Force: $$F_x=-\frac{dU}{dx}$$"]
    C --> G["Connect to $$\Delta K$$"]
    F --> H["Determine motion and equilibrium"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **net work** with the work done by a single force. The theorem is **$$W_{\text{net}}=\Delta K$$**, not necessarily the work of just one force.
- Forgetting the **sign** of work: a force opposite the displacement does **negative work**.
- Using **$$U_g = mgh$$** without defining a consistent reference level; only **changes** in potential energy matter physically.
- Assuming energy is always conserved mechanically even when **friction** or an external force is present. In that case, include **$$W_{nc}$$**.
- Misreading graphs: the **area under $$F$$ vs. $$x$$** is work, but for **$$U$$ vs. $$x$$**, it is the **slope**, not the area, that determines force.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can compute **work** from a constant force using $$W=\vec{F}\cdot\Delta\vec{r}$$.
- [ ] I can evaluate work for a **variable force** using $$W=\int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$$ or area under an **$$F_x$$ vs. $$x$$** graph.
- [ ] I can apply the **work–kinetic energy theorem** to connect force and speed.
- [ ] I can distinguish **conservative** and **nonconservative** forces and know when **potential energy** can be defined.
- [ ] I can use **$$U_g=mgy$$** and **$$U_s=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$$** correctly in energy problems.
- [ ] I can solve problems using **$$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f$$** when mechanical energy is conserved.
- [ ] I can include friction or external work using **$$W_{nc}=\Delta K+\Delta U$$**.
- [ ] I can calculate **average** and **instantaneous power**, including **$$P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$**.
- [ ] I can interpret **$$U(x)$$** graphs to find force and identify equilibrium points.

flashcards.definition: The energy transfer associated with a force acting through a displacement, computed by integrating the component of the force along the path: $$W=\int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$$.
The scalar operation that selects the component of a vector parallel to another vector; in mechanics it gives $$Fd\cos\theta$$ for an infinitesimal displacement.
The quantity associated with motion of a particle, equal to $$\tfrac12 mv^2$$ for nonrelativistic speeds.
The principle stating that the net energy transfer by forces equals the change in the motion-related scalar quantity: $$W_{\text{net}}=\Delta K$$.
For one-dimensional motion, the signed region between the force curve and the position axis over an interval, which gives $$\int F_x\,dx$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A particle moves along the $$x$$-axis from $$x=0$$ to $$x=2\,\text{m}$$ under a force $$F_x(x)=3x^2-4x\,\text{N}$$. What is the work done by this force on the particle?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: According to the work–kinetic energy theorem, the net work done on a particle is equal to ______.
For motion along one dimension, the work done by a position-dependent force from $$x=a$$ to $$x=b$$ is given by ______.

flashcards.definition: A scalar function associated with a conservative interaction such that changes in it are the negative of the work done by that interaction: $$\Delta U=-W_{\text{cons}}$$.
An interaction for which the work between two points is path independent and the net work around any closed loop is zero.
When only conservative interactions do work, the sum $$K+U$$ remains constant, so $$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f$$.
The rate at which energy is transferred at a particular moment, given by $$P=\dfrac{dW}{dt}=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$$.
The stored energy in an ideal spring displaced from equilibrium, equal to $$\tfrac12 kx^2$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A particle moves in one dimension under the conservative force $$F_x(x)=-4x^3\,\text{N}$$, where $$x$$ is in meters. If $$U(0)=0$$, what is the potential energy function?

A force on a particle is $$\vec{F}=(6x\,\hat{i})\,\text{N}$$. The particle passes through $$x=2\,\text{m}$$ with velocity $$\vec{v}=(3\,\hat{i}+4\,\hat{j})\,\text{m/s}$$. What is the instantaneous power delivered by the force at that instant?

units.note:
# Unit 4: Systems of Particles and Linear Momentum

## Overview
This unit develops the mechanics of **multiple-particle systems** by focusing on **center of mass**, **linear momentum**, **impulse**, and **collisions**. These ideas are essential on the AP Physics C exam because they connect **Newton’s laws**, **calculus-based force analysis**, and **conservation principles** in situations where energy alone is not enough.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **System of particles** | A collection of objects treated together as one overall system. | AP problems often ask you to choose a system so you can decide whether **momentum** is conserved. |
| **Center of mass** | The weighted-average position of all mass in a system. | You may need to find the motion of a complicated system by tracking only the **center of mass**. |
| **Linear momentum** | The product of mass and velocity: a vector quantity. | Central to free-response and multiple-choice questions involving interactions, recoil, and collisions. |
| **Impulse** | The integral of force over time; equal to change in momentum. | AP Physics C frequently connects **variable force** and **momentum change** using calculus. |
| **Conservation of momentum** | Total momentum of an isolated system remains constant. | One of the most tested tools for explosions, recoil, and collisions. |
| **Elastic vs. inelastic collisions** | In **elastic** collisions, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in **inelastic** collisions, only momentum is conserved. | Students must identify which conservation laws apply in each scenario. |
| **Perfectly inelastic collision** | A collision in which objects stick together after impact. | A common AP setup requiring momentum conservation but **not** kinetic energy conservation. |
| **Variable-mass systems** | Systems whose mass changes with time, such as rockets ejecting fuel. | AP questions may test careful use of momentum ideas when mass is not constant. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Choose the system] --> B[Identify external forces]
    B --> C{"Is net external impulse negligible?"}
    C -->|Yes| D[Use conservation of total momentum]
    C -->|No| E[Use impulse-momentum theorem]
    D --> F[Relate velocities before and after interaction]
    E --> F
    F --> G{"Collision type?"}
    G -->|Elastic| H[Also conserve kinetic energy]
    G -->|Inelastic| I[Do not conserve kinetic energy]
    G -->|Perfectly inelastic| J[Set final velocities equal]
    H --> K[Solve for unknowns]
    I --> K
    J --> K
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Idea** | **Equation / Rule** |
|---|---|
| **Linear momentum of a particle** | $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ |
| **Total momentum of a system** | $$\vec{P} = \sum \vec{p}_i = \sum m_i \vec{v}_i$$ |
| **Newton’s 2nd law in momentum form** | $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$$ |
| **Impulse** | $$\vec{J} = \int \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\,dt$$ |
| **Impulse-momentum theorem** | $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{P} = \vec{P}_f - \vec{P}_i$$ |
| **Conservation of momentum** | If $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$$ over the interval, then $$\vec{P}_i = \vec{P}_f$$ |
| **Center of mass position** | $$\vec{r}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M}\sum m_i \vec{r}_i$$ where $$M = \sum m_i$$ |
| **Center of mass velocity** | $$\vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{d\vec{r}_{\text{cm}}}{dt} = \frac{1}{M}\sum m_i \vec{v}_i$$ |
| **Center of mass acceleration** | $$\vec{a}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M}\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}}$$ |
| **Elastic collision rule** | Conserve both $$\vec{P}$$ and $$K$$ |
| **Kinetic energy** | $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ |
| **Perfectly inelastic collision** | Conserve momentum and set shared final velocity: $$m_1\vec{v}_{1i} + m_2\vec{v}_{2i} = (m_1 + m_2)\vec{v}_f$$ |
| **1D elastic collision shortcut** | Relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation: $$v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$$ |
| **Variable-mass momentum idea** | For systems like rockets, apply momentum conservation carefully to the system including expelled mass, or use $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$$ |

### Must-know exam rules
- **Momentum is always conserved only for an isolated system** or when net external impulse is zero.
- **Kinetic energy is not generally conserved** in collisions.
- Internal forces may be large, but they do **not** change the total momentum of the system.
- The **center of mass** moves as if all external force acted on a single particle of mass $$M$$.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Similarities** | **Differences / AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Impulse** vs. **Momentum** | Both are vector quantities and linked by $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{P}$$. | **Momentum** is a state quantity; **impulse** describes the effect of force over time. AP often gives a **force-time graph** and asks for area. |
| **Elastic** vs. **Inelastic collision** | Both conserve total momentum in an isolated system. | Only **elastic** collisions conserve kinetic energy. In **inelastic** collisions, some kinetic energy becomes thermal, sound, or deformation energy. |
| **Particle motion** vs. **Center-of-mass motion** | Both use position, velocity, and acceleration. | Individual particles may move unpredictably, but the **center of mass** follows only the net external force. |
| **Constant-mass** vs. **Variable-mass systems** | Both rely on momentum principles. | In **variable-mass** systems, you must define the system carefully and cannot blindly use $$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$$ with constant $$m$$ assumptions. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[External force present] --> B[Changes total system momentum]
    C[Internal force only] --> D[Does not change total system momentum]
    B --> E[Center of mass accelerates]
    D --> F[Center of mass motion unchanged by internal interaction alone]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **momentum conservation** with **kinetic energy conservation**. In most collisions, momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.
- Forgetting that **momentum is a vector**. In one dimension, choose a sign convention; in two dimensions, conserve momentum separately in the $$x$$ and $$y$$ directions.
- Applying momentum conservation when there is a significant **external impulse**, such as friction acting over a measurable time interval.
- Treating **perfectly inelastic** collisions as energy-conserving just because the objects stick together. Sticking means kinetic energy decreases.
- Using **center of mass** formulas without accounting for all masses in the system, or mixing particle coordinates with center-of-mass coordinates.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can define **linear momentum** and explain why it is a **vector**.
- [ ] I can use $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$$ and the **impulse-momentum theorem** in calculus-based situations.
- [ ] I can calculate **impulse** from a constant force, a variable force, or the area under a **force-time graph**.
- [ ] I can determine when **momentum is conserved** by analyzing the system and external forces.
- [ ] I can find the **center of mass** position or velocity of a system of particles.
- [ ] I can solve **elastic**, **inelastic**, and **perfectly inelastic** collision problems.
- [ ] I can distinguish when **kinetic energy** is conserved and when it is not.
- [ ] I can explain the key idea behind **variable-mass systems**, especially rockets or mass ejection situations.

flashcards.term: Center of mass of a system
flashcards.definition: The weighted-average position of all mass in a collection of objects, given by $$\vec r_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_i m_i \vec r_i$$ for discrete masses or $$\vec r_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{M}\int \vec r\,dm$$ for a continuous distribution.

flashcards.term: Translational form of Newton's second law for a system
flashcards.definition: For a collection of particles, the net external force equals the time rate of change of total momentum and also equals total mass times the acceleration of the weighted-average position when mass is constant: $$\sum \vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac{d\vec p_{\mathrm{sys}}}{dt}=M\vec a_{\mathrm{cm}}$$.
The vector sum of the momenta of all particles in the collection: $$\vec p_{\mathrm{sys}}=\sum_i m_i \vec v_i$$. If the net external force is zero, this quantity remains constant.
The time integral of the net external force over an interval, equal to the change in total momentum: $$\vec J=\int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}\,dt=\Delta \vec p$$.
When the vector sum of external forces is zero over an interaction, the total momentum before the interaction equals the total momentum after it: $$\vec p_i=\vec p_f$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A uniform rod of length $$L$$ lies along the $$x$$-axis from $$x=0$$ to $$x=L$$. A point mass $$m$$ is attached at $$x=0$$, and an identical point mass $$m$$ is attached at $$x=L$$. The rod has mass $$2m$$. What is the position of the system's center of mass measured from $$x=0$$?
A net external force on a system varies with time as $$F(t)=kt$$ in the $$+x$$ direction for $$0\le t\le T$$. If the system's initial momentum is zero, what is its momentum at time $$T$$?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For any system of particles, the net external force satisfies $$\sum \vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac{d}{dt}(\,\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\,)$$. The blank is best filled by ______.
If the net external force on a system is zero, then the velocity of the center of mass remains ______.

flashcards.definition: An interaction in which total momentum is conserved and total kinetic energy is also conserved. In one dimension, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach.
An interaction in which objects stick together after impact. Total momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases by the maximum amount possible for a given initial momentum.

A dimensionless ratio for a collision, defined in one dimension as the relative speed after impact divided by the relative speed before impact: $$e=\frac{|v_{2f}-v_{1f}|}{|v_{1i}-v_{2i}|}$$, with $$e=1$$ for kinetic-energy-conserving impacts and $$e=0$$ when objects leave with the same final velocity.

For a body that changes mass by expelling material, the speed change relative to an inertial frame satisfies $$\Delta v=v_{\mathrm{ex}}\ln\!\left(\frac{m_i}{m_f}\right)$$ when external forces are negligible and the exhaust speed relative to the body is constant.

The force on a mass-ejecting vehicle due to expelled material, commonly modeled as $$F_{\mathrm{thrust}}=\left|\frac{dm}{dt}\right|v_{\mathrm{ex}}$$ when exhaust speed relative to the vehicle is constant.

multipleChoice.questionText: A block of mass $$m$$ moving with speed $$v$$ on a frictionless surface collides and sticks to an identical block initially at rest. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy remains as kinetic energy immediately after the collision?

A rocket in deep space experiences negligible external forces and ejects fuel with constant exhaust speed $$v_{\mathrm{ex}}$$ relative to the rocket. Its mass decreases from $$M$$ to $$\frac{M}{e^2}$$. What is the magnitude of the rocket's change in speed?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In a one-dimensional collision, if total momentum and total kinetic energy are both conserved, the collision is classified as ______.
For a rocket with negligible external forces, integrating $$M\,d v=-v_{\mathrm{ex}}\,dM$$ leads to $$\Delta v=v_{\mathrm{ex}}\ln\left(\frac{______}{m_f}\right)$$.

units.note:
# Unit 5: Rotation, Oscillations, and Gravitation

## Overview
This unit extends Newtonian mechanics to **rotational motion**, **oscillatory motion**, and **gravitation**. You’ll learn how forces cause objects to rotate, why many systems naturally oscillate, and how gravity governs motion from falling objects to planetary orbits—all of which are frequent targets for both **multiple-choice** and **free-response** questions on the AP Physics C: Mechanics exam.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Torque** | The rotational analogue of force; measures how strongly a force tends to cause rotation about an axis. | AP questions often require setting up **net torque** equations and choosing the correct **lever arm**. |
| **Rotational Dynamics** | The relationship between torque, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration. | Central to solving rigid-body motion problems using $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$. |
| **Moment of Inertia** | A measure of how mass is distributed relative to an axis of rotation. | Students must compare rotational resistance for different shapes and apply the correct $$I$$ formula. |
| **Angular Momentum** | Rotational analogue of linear momentum; depends on rotational inertia and angular velocity. | Conservation of angular momentum is a major AP theme, especially in collision and spinning-body problems. |
| **Rolling Motion** | Combined translational and rotational motion, often without slipping. | AP problems frequently connect $$v$$, $$\omega$$, translational energy, and rotational energy. |
| **Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)** | Oscillatory motion in which restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium. | You must identify SHM conditions and use period, energy, and force relationships. |
| **Gravitational Force and Field** | Universal attractive force between masses and the field it creates. | Appears in orbit, satellite, and planetary motion problems using Newton’s law of gravitation. |
| **Circular/Orbital Motion** | Motion sustained by a centripetal force, often provided by gravity. | AP often links gravitation with uniform circular motion to derive orbital speed or period. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Identify system and axis of rotation"] --> B["Draw force diagram"]
    B --> C["Find lever arms and torque signs"]
    C --> D["Apply $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$"]
    D --> E["Relate angular variables using rotational kinematics or dynamics"]
    E --> F["If rolling, use $$v = \omega R$$"]
    F --> G["If energy is involved, use translational + rotational energy"]

    H["Oscillation system"] --> I["Check for restoring force proportional to displacement"]
    I --> J["Model as SHM"]
    J --> K["Use $$a = -\omega^2 x$$, period, and energy relations"]

    L["Gravitational interaction"] --> M["Use $$F_g = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$"]
    M --> N["For orbit, set gravity equal to centripetal force"]
    N --> O["Solve for $$v$$, $$T$$, or $$r$$"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Topic** | **Formula / Rule** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Angular Kinematics** | $$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$$ | Angular velocity under constant angular acceleration |
|  | $$\theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$$ | Angular displacement under constant $$\alpha$$ |
|  | $$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(\theta - \theta_0)$$ | Rotational analogue of linear kinematics |
| **Torque** | $$\tau = rF\sin\phi$$ | Magnitude of torque from a force |
| **Rotational Dynamics** | $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$ | Newton’s second law for rotation |
| **Moment of Inertia** | $$I = \sum mr^2$$ | Point-mass definition |
|  | $$I_{\text{disk}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$$ | Solid disk or cylinder about center |
|  | $$I_{\text{hoop}} = MR^2$$ | Hoop or ring about center |
|  | $$I_{\text{rod, center}} = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$$ | Thin rod about center |
|  | $$I_{\text{rod, end}} = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$$ | Thin rod about one end |
| **Angular Momentum** | $$L = I\omega$$ | Rotating rigid body |
|  | $$\sum \tau = \frac{dL}{dt}$$ | Torque changes angular momentum |
|  | $$L_i = L_f$$ | Conserved if net external torque is zero |
| **Rolling Without Slipping** | $$v_{\text{cm}} = \omega R$$ | Links translational and rotational motion |
| **Rotational Energy** | $$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$ | Kinetic energy of rotation |
| **Total Kinetic Energy (rolling)** | $$K = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$ | Used in rolling energy problems |
| **Hooke’s Law** | $$F = -kx$$ | Restoring force for a spring |
| **SHM Acceleration** | $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ | Defining feature of SHM |
| **Spring-Mass Period** | $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$ | Period of mass-spring oscillator |
| **Pendulum Period** | $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$ | Small-angle simple pendulum only |
| **SHM Energy** | $$E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$ | Mechanical energy in ideal spring SHM |
| **Newton’s Law of Gravitation** | $$F_g = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$ | Universal gravitational attraction |
| **Gravitational Field** | $$g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$$ | Field strength due to a mass |
| **Gravitational Potential Energy** | $$U_g = -\frac{GMm}{r}$$ | Zero at infinity |
| **Circular Orbit Speed** | $$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$ | Speed for a circular orbit |
| **Orbital Period** | $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$$ | Circular orbital period |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Force vs. Torque** | Both cause acceleration and follow Newton-style laws. | Force causes **linear acceleration**: $$\sum F = ma$$; torque causes **angular acceleration**: $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$. |
| **Mass vs. Moment of Inertia** | Each resists acceleration. | Mass resists linear motion; **moment of inertia** resists rotational motion and depends on mass distribution relative to the axis. |
| **Linear Momentum vs. Angular Momentum** | Both are conserved when the corresponding external influence is zero. | Linear momentum is conserved when **net external force** is zero; angular momentum is conserved when **net external torque** is zero. |
| **Uniform Circular Motion vs. SHM** | Both involve acceleration and periodic ideas. | Circular motion has inward **centripetal acceleration**; SHM has restoring acceleration proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **radius** with **lever arm**: in torque problems, use the **perpendicular distance** from the axis to the force’s line of action.
- Using $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$ when the object is actually in **rotational equilibrium**; if angular acceleration is zero, then $$\sum \tau = 0$$.
- Forgetting that **rolling without slipping** requires $$v_{\text{cm}} = \omega R$$, not just rotation and translation independently.
- Applying the pendulum formula $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$ for large angles; on AP Physics C, this is valid only for **small-angle** oscillations.
- Treating gravitational potential energy near Earth as always $$mgh$$; for planetary/orbital situations, use $$U_g = -\frac{GMm}{r}$$ instead.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can calculate **torque** and determine its sign about a chosen axis.
- [ ] I can apply $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$ to solve rotational dynamics problems.
- [ ] I know common **moment of inertia** formulas and can choose the correct one.
- [ ] I can use **conservation of angular momentum** in spinning and collision scenarios.
- [ ] I can solve **rolling without slipping** problems using energy or kinematics.
- [ ] I can identify whether a system undergoes **simple harmonic motion** and find its **period**.
- [ ] I can use Newton’s law of **gravitation** to calculate force, field strength, or potential energy.
- [ ] I can connect **gravity** to **circular motion** to find orbital speed or orbital period.

flashcards.definition: A vector quantity that measures the rotational effect of a force about a chosen axis, given by $$\vec{\tau}=\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$$, with magnitude $$\tau=rF\sin\theta$$.
A measure of how mass is distributed relative to an axis of rotation, determining resistance to angular acceleration, expressed for discrete masses as $$I=\sum mr^2$$.

flashcards.term: Rotational Form of Newton's Second Law
flashcards.definition: The relationship stating that the net external rotational effect on a rigid body equals the product of its rotational inertia and angular acceleration: $$\sum \tau = I\alpha$$.
The rotational analog of linear momentum; for a particle it is $$\vec{L}=\vec{r}\times\vec{p}$$, and for a rigid body about a fixed axis it is $$L=I\omega$$.
The condition in which translational and rotational motion are linked so that the point of contact is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface, requiring $$v_{\text{cm}}=\omega R$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A uniform disk and a hoop have the same mass and radius and are released from rest at the top of identical inclines, rolling without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
options: The uniform disk, because it has a smaller moment of inertia relative to $$MR^2$$
The hoop, because more rotational kinetic energy increases its acceleration
They arrive simultaneously, because mechanical energy is conserved for both
The hoop, because static friction does positive work on it
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The uniform disk, because it has a smaller moment of inertia relative to $$MR^2$$

multipleChoice.questionText: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis. If the net external torque on the body is zero, which statement must be true?
options: Its angular momentum about the axis remains constant
Its rotational kinetic energy must decrease
Its moment of inertia must remain constant
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Its angular momentum about the axis remains constant

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For a particle of mass $$m$$ moving in a circle of radius $$r$$ with speed $$v$$, the magnitude of its angular momentum about the center is $$L=______$$.
For an object rolling without slipping, the speed of the center of mass is related to angular speed by $$v_{\text{cm}}=______$$.

flashcards.definition: Periodic motion in which the restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction, leading to $$a=-\omega^2x$$.

flashcards.term: Angular Frequency of a Mass-Spring System
flashcards.definition: For an ideal oscillator consisting of a mass attached to a spring, the rate parameter of oscillation is $$\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$$.
For small angular displacements, the time for one complete oscillation is $$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$$.
The attractive interaction between two point masses is given by $$F_g=G\dfrac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$ and acts along the line joining them.
For two masses separated by distance $$r$$ and taking zero at infinity, the energy associated with their interaction is $$U=-G\dfrac{m_1m_2}{r}$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: A block of mass $$m$$ attached to an ideal spring oscillates horizontally with amplitude $$A$$. At displacement $$x$$ from equilibrium, which expression gives its speed?
A satellite moves in a stable circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a planet of mass $$M$$. Which expression gives the satellite's orbital speed?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: For a mass-spring oscillator, the restoring force is $$F=______$$.
For small-angle oscillations of a simple pendulum, the period is $$T=______$$.
